<reason>A (CON) won the central clashes. A's counterfactual frame — the real alternative is a five-day week with a vacant algebra seat — was never squarely defeated; B's answer ("the calendar can't outbid $15k") was adequately met by A's compensating-differentials point that teachers trading salary for schedule IS the retention the motion names. A demolished B's signature "money or hours, not both" trap using B's own opening concession that savings sit in operational lines, forcing B into a graceful retreat ("I never denied something shrinks; I denied it matters"). A's averaging reconciliation (near-zero net effects = longer-day costs offset by filled-classroom gains) answered B's sharpest question and was never re-engaged; attendance stood unrebutted from the opening; and A's concrete tutoring-transport answer (one van, one wing) was ignored in B's closing. B was the better stylist — "an engine that never moves the car," the ceiling/asymmetry frame — but its harms rested on asserted compression-in-practice rather than evidence, and its strongest mechanisms were subsumed by A's unchallenged characterization of the research. Costs: A clipped two turns and trimmed B4.3's quote in the closing to imply a concession B didn't make; B clipped its opening and twice claimed questions were "unanswered" that were then or already answered. Net: A's substantive path survived more intact.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 1 [A2.1]+[A2.4]: collapsing B's "money or hours, not both" trap by pointing out savings live in the fifth day's buses/heat/cafeteria (which B's own opening conceded) while hours are preserved by lengthening four days — then reversing the compounding frame: "zero compounded over twelve years is zero; what compounds is the vacancy." B never rebuilt the trap, only downgraded it to a magnitude claim.</best_rebuttal>
